newsitem.title: USA: House panel clears CIA of role in Guatemala deaths.
newsitem.headline: House panel clears CIA of role in Guatemala deaths.

text.p: The House Intelligence Committee on Monday cleared the CIA of involvement in the killing in Guatemala of an American and a Guatemalan guerrilla leader married to an American lawyer.
The charge was made two years ago by New Jersey Democratic Sen. Robert Torricelli, then a member of the House of Representatives.

Torricelli, in a letter to President Bill Clinton and in public statements, accused the Central Intelligence Agency of "direct involvement" in the 1990 murder of American Michael DeVine, who ran a hotel in Guatemala, and Efraim Bamaca Velasquez, who disappeared while a prisoner of the Guatemalan military in 1992.
The Bamaca case became a cause celebre when his widow, Jennifer Harbury, a Harvard Law School graduate, conducted hunger strikes to try to learn the truth about his disappearance.
Torricelli, then a member of the Intelligence Committee, said the CIA found out the killings were ordered by a Guatemalan colonel on its payroll but concealed its knowledge.

In a majority report on its 18-month investigation, the House committee said: "There is no evidence to suppport the allegations that United States government personnel in any way directed or participated in the DeVine death, or the capture, interrogation or subsequent disappearance of Bamaca."
It said it found "none of the allegations" about CIA involvement raised by Torricelli in his letter to Clinton or in later public statements "have proven to be true."
In a minority report, four of the committee's Democrats said they did not agree with this statement, saying it was not supported by the evidence the committee had seen.

A statement issued by Torricelli's office said the senator "stands by his actions and the general accuracy of his contentions about illegal and shameful conduct by the Central Intelligence Agency in Central America."

The committee also said allegations by Torricelli that two U.S. Army officers were involved in purging records that showed possible involvement of U.S. Army intelligence in the two deaths had proven not to be true.
Torricelli had relied on an anonymous source for this charge. The committee said it had been told that a federal grand jury was considering charges concerning fabrication of the allegations.

The report said the committee found no reason to dispute an Intelligence Oversight Board conclusion that several CIA "assets" were credibly alleged to have participated in human rights violations, including assassination and torture.

The committee also said that CIA leaders had violated the requirement to keep congressional intelligence committees informed of its ties with the Guatemala military and the human rights problems of some of its intelligence contacts.
